content: For vaccination programs, it is essential to maintain routine monthly or quarterly calculations of coverage. This should include not only the coverage of vaccinations but also the coverage of one or more interventions within the integrated service. Monitoring measures, such as defaulter tracing, can be utilized to combine questions related to both immunization and integrated services, providing a more comprehensive understanding of service delivery. It is critical to compare interventions that are expected to have similar coverage levels, such as birth doses of BCG and hepatitis B vaccines, as well as skilled birth attendance. These comparisons can help identify opportunities or gaps in the delivery of integrated services. Service delivery and coverage levels should ideally be reviewed on a monthly basis. However, improvements may initially be slow due to the time required for health workers and communities to adapt to integrated services. Monthly monitoring is beneficial for tracking changes in service inputs and delivery, identifying increases in activity that may indicate improved coverage, and detecting decreases in activity that could suggest negative impacts on service provision or acceptance. When monitoring service delivery, it is important to revisit the original objectives of the immunization and integrated services, particularly if their target populations differ. Additionally, services with different timing requirements, such as seasonal malaria control activities, should be considered. In such cases, comparing monthly rates with the same month in a previous year may be more appropriate than month-to-month comparisons. Integrated services often add new responsibilities for existing health workers, making it necessary to monitor their workload. Regular assessments of the quality of immunization sessions and integrated services are also important. This can be achieved through standard reporting, structured supervision, or the use of specific tools like immunization session checklists. Supportive supervision visits to health facilities can facilitate the monitoring of changes resulting from integrated services. These visits can include additional questions on supervision checklists to gather health workers’ or beneficiaries’ opinions on the benefits and challenges of integrated services. Baseline data is crucial for evaluating the impact of integrated services, as it provides a reference point for comparing service delivery performance before and after integration. Evaluations should be agreed upon by all relevant programs early on and can be conducted through dedicated program evaluations, post-introduction evaluations of new vaccines, or as part of broader program reviews. Evaluations should involve immunization program managers, managers of integrated services, central planning health workers, and other stakeholders, such as development partners and WHO/UNICEF advisors. Including supervisors or frontline health workers can provide valuable field perspectives. Evaluations should utilize available monitoring data and may require the collection of additional data. To strengthen the evidence base for integration, more empirical research is needed to determine what works, using scientifically valid implementation research methods. While research is not always necessary, it is appropriate when questions arise about the implementation, impact, or cost-effectiveness of integration. Strong monitoring and evaluation efforts can ensure successful implementation and provide valuable insights for other countries. Growth monitoring and nutrition counseling are often linked with immunization services, providing frequent contact with health workers and enabling access to child health interventions. Immunization sessions also offer opportunities for growth monitoring, nutrition counseling, and breastfeeding support. Health education, including breastfeeding information, can be provided to pregnant women during antenatal care. The WHO has established child growth standards, such as length/height-for-age and weight-for-age, which are incorporated into home-based records in many countries. These indicators help monitor healthy growth, ensure timely screening and treatment of undernutrition, and promote appropriate nutritional practices. The Global Strategy for Infant and Young Child Feeding emphasizes the importance of protecting, promoting, and supporting healthy growth and nutrition. It recommends comprehensive national policies to foster environments that support appropriate feeding practices. Skilled counseling and support for infant and young child feeding should be provided during well-baby clinics, immunization sessions, and other health services. Infants should be exclusively breastfed for the first six months of life to achieve optimal growth, development, and health. After six months, they should receive nutritionally adequate and safe complementary foods while breastfeeding continues for up to two years or beyond. A nurturing care framework will be launched to build on evidence of effective interventions for child development.
